title: Sequence Clustering
text: distance metric defines (dis)similarity sequences measured. words, quantifies different two sequences . Nestimate currently supports 9 distance metrics comparing sequences: Different metrics may produce different clustering results. need choose based research question: Hamming: compares sequences position position (best aligned sequences equal length). Edit distances (lv, osa, dl): allow insertions deletions (best sequences may shifted vary length). LCS: captures shared subsequences (best overall patterns matter exact alignment). can specify distance metric want use dissimilarity argument: distance metrics may take additional arguments. example, Hamming distance accepts temporal weighting emphasize earlier later positions:
code: # Levenshtein distance (allows insertions/deletions) clust_lv <- build_clusters(net, k = 3, dissimilarity = "lv") clust_lv #> Sequence Clustering [pam] #>   Sequences: 526  |  Clusters: 3 #>   Dissimilarity: lv #>   Quality: silhouette = 0.269 #>  #>   Cluster  N            Mean within-dist  Medoid #>   1        228 (43.3%)  9.588             245 #>   2        183 (34.8%)  4.278             46 #>   3        115 (21.9%)  34.472            420  # Longest common subsequence clust_lcs <- build_clusters(net, k = 3, dissimilarity = "lcs") clust_lcs #> Sequence Clustering [pam] #>   Sequences: 526  |  Clusters: 3 #>   Dissimilarity: lcs #>   Quality: silhouette = 0.184 #>  #>   Cluster  N            Mean within-dist  Medoid #>   1        185 (35.2%)  5.730             511 #>   2        91 (17.3%)   42.419            420 #>   3        250 (47.5%)  13.577            325 # Emphasize earlier positions (higher lambda = faster decay) clust_weighted <- build_clusters(net,                                 k = 3,                                dissimilarity = "hamming",                                weighted = TRUE,                                lambda = 0.5) clust_weighted #> Sequence Clustering [pam] #>   Sequences: 526  |  Clusters: 3 #>   Dissimilarity: hamming (weighted, lambda = 0.5) #>   Quality: silhouette = 0.234 #>  #>   Cluster  N            Mean within-dist  Medoid #>   1        192 (36.5%)  0.623             492 #>   2        303 (57.6%)  0.667             316 #>   3        31 ( 5.9%)   0.946             525

title: Sequence Clustering
text: default, Nestimate uses PAM (Partitioning Around Medoids) form clusters, assigns sequence cluster represented central sequence (medoid). Besides PAM, Nestimate supports hierarchical clustering methods, build clusters step step progressively merging similar units tree-like structure (dendrogram): ward.D2 (“Ward’s Method, Squared Distances”): Minimizes increase within-cluster variance using squared distances. Typically produces compact, well-separated clusters. ward.D (“Ward’s Method”): alternative implementation Ward’s approach using different distance formulation. Similar behavior, results may vary slightly. complete (“Complete Linkage”): Defines distance clusters maximum distance members. Produces tight, compact clusters. average (“Average Linkage”): Uses average distance pairs points across clusters. Provides balance compactness flexibility. single (“Single Linkage”): Uses minimum distance points two clusters. Can capture chain-like structures may lead - loosely connected clusters. mcquitty (“McQuitty’s Method” / “WPGMA”): weighted version average linkage gives equal weight clusters regardless size. centroid (“Centroid Linkage”): Defines cluster distance based distance cluster centroids (means). Can produce intuitive groupings may introduce inconsistencies hierarchy. use methods instead PAM, need provide method argument build_clusters.
code: # Ward's method (minimizes within-cluster variance) clust_ward <- build_clusters(net, k = 3, method = "ward.D2") clust_ward #> Sequence Clustering [ward.D2] #>   Sequences: 526  |  Clusters: 3 #>   Dissimilarity: hamming #>   Quality: silhouette = 0.569 #>  #>   Cluster  N            Mean within-dist #>   1        435 (82.7%)  13.148 #>   2        83 (15.8%)   38.666 #>   3        8 ( 1.5%)    92.964  # Complete linkage clust_complete <- build_clusters(net, k = 3, method = "complete") clust_complete #> Sequence Clustering [complete] #>   Sequences: 526  |  Clusters: 3 #>   Dissimilarity: hamming #>   Quality: silhouette = 0.802 #>  #>   Cluster  N            Mean within-dist #>   1        518 (98.5%)  21.523 #>   2        7 ( 1.3%)    87.524 #>   3        1 ( 0.2%)    0.000

title: Sequence Clustering
text: Instead clustering sequences based similar one another, can cluster together based transition dynamics. Mixture Markov models (MMM) fit separate Markov models, sequences assigned cluster whose transition structure best matches observed behavior. implement MMM, can use build_mmm(), returns net_mmm object full model details: net_mmm object contains posterior probabilities, model fit statistics (BIC, AIC, ICL), one transition matrix per cluster; build_network(mmm_fit) turns per-cluster networks (see ). cluster_diagnostics() works , MMM-specific columns (mixing share, average posterior probability, per-cluster classification error): posterior plot type shows distribution sequence’s max posterior probability, faceted cluster. Tight distributions near 1 indicate clean assignment; spread-distributions indicate fuzzy clusters.
code: mmm_fit <- build_mmm(net, k = 2) summary(mmm_fit) #> Mixed Markov Model #>   Sequences: 526  |  Clusters: 2  |  States: 3 #>   ICs: LL = -10074.921  |  BIC = 20256.351  |  AIC = 20183.841  |  ICL = 20536.529 #>   Quality: AvePP = 0.782  |  Entropy = 0.642  |  Class.Err = 21.8% #>  #>   Cluster  N            Mix%   AvePP #>   1        334 (63.5%)  55.7%  0.766 #>   2        192 (36.5%)  44.3%  0.808 #>  #> --- Cluster 1 (55.7%, n=334) --- #>               Directive Evaluative Metacognitive #> Directive         0.647      0.144         0.208 #> Evaluative        0.549      0.269         0.181 #> Metacognitive     0.429      0.257         0.314 #>  #> --- Cluster 2 (44.3%, n=192) --- #>               Directive Evaluative Metacognitive #> Directive         0.565      0.301         0.134 #> Evaluative        0.447      0.462         0.090 #> Metacognitive     0.398      0.435         0.166 #>   component     prior n_assigned mean_posterior     avepp #> 1         1 0.5566997        334      0.7663949 0.7663949 #> 2         2 0.4433003        192      0.8080413 0.8080413 diag_mmm <- cluster_diagnostics(mmm_fit) diag_mmm #> Cluster Diagnostics (mmm) [k = 2] #>   Sequences: 526  |  Clusters: 2  |  States: 3 #>   Quality: AvePP = 0.782  |  Entropy = 0.642  |  Class.Err = 21.8% #>   ICs: LL = -10074.921  |  BIC = 20256.351  |  AIC = 20183.841  |  ICL = 20536.529 #>  #>   Cluster  N            Mix%   AvePP  Class.Err% #>   1        334 (63.5%)  55.7%  0.766  23.4% #>   2        192 (36.5%)  44.3%  0.808  19.2% plot(diag_mmm, type = "posterior")

text: sequences grouped, goal usually compare transitions behave within group. single transition network estimated sequences averages across groups hides contrast. Estimating one network per cluster preserves group’s distinct dynamics — nodes, different edge weights. result netobject_group: list netobjects sharing node set, one per cluster. Every group network supports downstream operations single netobject — plotting via plot(), resampling via bootstrap_network(), group-level edge comparison via permutation(). Two paths produce netobject_group: Manual — fit clustering build_clusters() cluster_mmm(), pass fitted clustering build_network(). Shortcut — cluster_network() collapses fitting network materialization one call either distance MMM clustering. Distance clustering groups sessions sequence similarity. Model-based MMM clustering groups Markov model best explains sequence’s transitions.

title: Network Estimation and Visualization with Nestimate + cograph
text: Nestimate unified network estimation package R. provides single entry point — build_network() — accepts sequence data, wide-format behavioral data, numeric matrices estimates networks using 10 built-methods. result netobject inherits cograph_network, every object produced Nestimate can plotted splot() directly. core design principle estimation visualization separate concerns: Nestimate handles computation (network construction, bootstrapping, permutation testing, clustering, multi-cluster analysis), cograph handles rendering. separation means analyst writes estimation code gets publication-ready figures without adapter code manual class conversion. Beyond single-network estimation, Nestimate provides complete statistical toolkit: Bootstrap stability analysis (bootstrap_network) — identifies edges survive resampling sampling artifacts. Permutation-based group comparison (permutation) — tests whether edges differ significantly conditions. Multi-cluster multi-level analysis (csum, summarize_clusters) — aggregates node-level networks cluster-level summaries hierarchical visualization. Centrality stability (centrality_stability) — assesses whether centrality rankings robust case dropping. Group-level operations — bootstrapping, permutation testing, plotting work grouped networks additional code. tutorial walks full pipeline group_regulation_long dataset shipped Nestimate.

title: Higher-Order Network Analysis with Simplicial Complexes
text: analyze sequential data network — follows , state leads — typically build first-order Markov model: probability next state depends current state. foundation Transition Network Analysis (TNA). human behavior always memoryless. Consider two programmers working AI coding assistant: Programmer : Specify → Request → Specify → Request (steady back--forth) Programmer B: Frustrate → Specify → Request → Command (escalating frustration direct commands) first-order model, sequences contribute equally Specify → Request transition. context — came — matters. sequence Frustrate → Specify may lead different next actions Request → Specify. higher-order dependencies: cases past two () states jointly predict future better current state alone. tutorial introduces complete pipeline detecting, quantifying, visualizing higher-order structure sequential data. progress standard transition networks statistical order detection, pathway analysis, topology higher-order interactions using simplicial complexes. Test whether data higher-order dependencies (order) Identify specific pathways deviate first-order expectations Detect anomalously frequent rare behavioral sequences Compute topological invariants (Betti numbers, Euler characteristic) Track network topology changes across thresholds (persistent homology) Visualize higher-order pathways simplicial blob diagrams Compare higher-order structure across groups cograph provides simplicial visualization (plot_simplicial()). what: Is First-Order Enough? Multi-Order Model Selection
title: Higher-Order Network Analysis with Simplicial Complexes
text: investing higher-order analysis, answer: sequential memory actually matter? Multi-Order Generative Model (MOGen; Scholtes 2017) fits Markov models increasing orders compares using information criteria. Higher-order models fit better exponentially parameters — AIC BIC find best tradeoff.  plot traces AIC BIC functions Markov order. higher-order models always fit better terms raw log-likelihood (parameter space contains lower-order one), meaningful comparison fit complexity. AIC penalises parameter 2; BIC penalises log(n), dataset much larger 2 — BIC favors small orders much aggressively AIC. Order 0: Actions independent — sequential structure. Order 1: standard Markov model sufficient. Order 2+: Higher-order dependencies exist. first-order TNA miss . Even order 1 globally optimal (BIC), specific pathways may still exhibit higher-order behavior — global model averages states. HON analysis detects local patterns. next section adds complementary, principled hypothesis test often reveals signal BIC parsimonious flag. mogen_transitions() extracts transitions given order, showing two-step contexts lead different outcomes: row second-order pathway. column two-state context, predicted next state, count empirical frequency, probability conditional P(| ). high count combined high probability predictive context: knowing previous two states pins next one. high count low probability common ambiguous context — frequent data, successor distribution spread . plot_simplicial() accepts mogen_transitions() data.frame directly. takes top pathways count renders smooth blob shared circular layout, path’s intermediate states blue target state red. Repeated states (like Specify -> Command -> Specify) get distinct positions blob covers three visually distinct nodes rather collapsing line.  zoom single frequent pathway, set max_pathways = 1 let data.frame drive selection. mogen_transitions() returns rows already sorted count, max_pathways = N always picks top N:  MOGen uses information criteria. complementary approach permutation LRT markov_order_test(): order kk, tests H0H_0: “process order (k−1)(k-1)” H1H_1: “process order kk” reframing conditional-independence test (k+1)(k+1)-grams. null distribution built shuffling successor labels within context, needs plug-MLE approximation sparse (k+1)(k+1)-gram tables. permutation conditional rather exact: overlapping windows one sequence independent.  output reveals tension hidden single criterion. BIC selects smallest order (heavy parsimony penalty). AIC permutation LRT flag higher orders significantly better — every increase order yields G2G^2 statistic far tail within-context permutation null. right panel makes concrete: grey density null G2G^2 distribution per order, colored vertical line observed value. line sits right tail, H0H_0 rejected higher order carries genuine information beyond previous one. takeaway: sequential memory exists dataset. BIC penalises parameter space order 3 enormous (4,706 degrees freedom order-3 test alone), data pay cost. Order-selection answers global question. Transition entropy answers per-state question: predictable state’s next move? transition_entropy() computes Shannon row-entropy H(P[, ]) = -sum_j P[,j] log P[,j] every state, chain-level entropy rate h(P) = sum_i pi_i H(P[, ]) (Shannon-McMillan-Breiman per-step uncertainty stationary distribution pi), redundancy H(pi) - h(P) (much previous state reduces uncertainty next).  bar state’s outgoing-distribution entropy bits; bar’s width proportional stationary probability, visual area sums entropy rate h(P). dashed red line marks h(P); dotted line marks ceiling log_2(n) every state uniform outgoing distribution. States whose bar pokes near ceiling unpredictable hubs (next state essentially random); short bars deterministic — arrive , next step largely fixed.

code: data("group_regulation_long") net_GR <- build_network(group_regulation_long, method = "tna",                         action = "Action", actor = "Actor",                         time = "Time") # Default estimator = "auto" inspects the cluster x covariate cross-tab # and picks firth (brglm2, bias-reduced) only when rare cells signal # separation risk; otherwise it uses the much faster nnet::multinom. # With Achiever balanced 50/50, multinom is selected. Post <- build_clusters(net_GR, k = 2, covariates = c("Achiever")) summary(Post) #> Sequence Clustering Summary #>   Method:        pam  #>   Dissimilarity: hamming  #>   Silhouette:    0.1839  #>  #> Per-cluster statistics: #>  cluster size mean_within_dist #>        1  982         10.69340 #>        2 1018         18.59498 #>  #> Post-hoc Covariate Analysis (does not influence cluster membership)  #>  #> Cluster Profiles (categorical): #>  Cluster N    Achiever=High N(%) Achiever=Low N(%) #>  1        982 504 (51%)          478 (49%)         #>  2       1018 496 (49%)          522 (51%)         #>  #> Predictors of Membership (estimator = multinom, reference: Cluster 1): #>  Cluster Variable    OR   95% CI       p     Sig #>  2       AchieverLow 1.11 [0.93, 1.32] 0.245     #>  #> Model: AIC = 2774.6 | BIC = 2785.8 | McFadden R-squared = 0.00 #>  #> Note: Covariates are post-hoc and do not influence cluster assignments. title: Network Estimation and Analysis with Nestimate
text: Psychological network analysis estimates conditional dependency structure among set variables. Variables (e.g., symptoms, traits, behaviors) represented nodes, edges represent partial correlations — association two variables controlling others. approach reveals variables directly connected versus whose association mediated variables (Saqr et al., 2024). Nestimate supports three estimation methods continuous psychological data, accessed build_network() interface (binary data use method = "ising", mixed continuous categorical data method = "mgm"): Correlation networks (method = "cor") estimate pairwise Pearson correlations produce fully connected undirected networks. informative starting point, distinguish direct indirect associations. Partial correlation networks (method = "pcor") control variables, revealing direct associations. provide accurate picture dependency structure, though results can noisy small samples. Regularized networks via EBICglasso (method = "glasso") apply L1 regularization precision matrix, shrinking weak unreliable edges exactly zero. recommended approach psychological network analysis, balances model fit complexity produces sparse, interpretable, replicable structures.

text: chatgpt_srl dataset contains scale scores five self-regulated learning (SRL) constructs — Comprehension Study Understanding (CSU), Intrinsic Value (IV), Self-Efficacy (SE), Self-Regulation (SR), Task Avoidance (TA) — 1,000 responses generated ChatGPT validated SRL questionnaire (Vogelsmeier et al., 2025).

title: Network Estimation and Analysis with Nestimate
text: graphical lasso applies L1 regularization precision matrix (inverse covariance matrix), producing sparse network weak unreliable edges shrunk exactly zero. gamma parameter controls sparsity EBIC model selection — higher values yield sparser networks.
code: net_glasso <- build_network(chatgpt_srl, method = "glasso",                             params = list(gamma = 0.5)) net_glasso #> Partial Correlation Network (EBICglasso) [undirected] #>   Sample size: 1000 #>  #>   Weight matrix: #>       CSU IV SE SR TA #>   CSU   0  0  0  0  0 #>   IV    0  0  0  0  0 #>   SE    0  0  0  0  0 #>   SR    0  0  0  0  0 #>   TA    0  0  0  0  0  #>  #>   Predictability (R²): #>   CSU           0.000   #>   IV            0.000   #>   SE            0.000   #>   SR            0.000   #>   TA            0.000   #>  #>   Gamma: 0.50  |  Lambda: 0.0517

code: library(Nestimate)  net <- build_network(human_long, method = "tna",                      action = "code", actor = "session_id", time = "timestamp")  # Per-group networks in one call: high vs low achievers group_nets <- build_network(group_regulation_long, method = "tna",                             action = "Action", actor = "Actor",                             time = "Time", group = "Achiever")

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: wtna() builds networks binary (one-hot) data using temporal windows — directed transitions windows, undirected co-occurrence within windows, mixed network combining .
code: net_wtna  <- wtna(learning_activities, actor = "student",                   method = "transition", type = "relative") net_mixed <- wtna(learning_activities, actor = "student",                   method = "both", type = "relative")

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: cooccurrence() builds undirected co-occurrence networks 6 input formats (delimited fields, long/bipartite, binary matrix, wide sequence, lists) 8 similarity methods (Jaccard, cosine, association strength, Dice, ).
code: # From a long-format data frame: codes co-occurring within a session net_co <- cooccurrence(human_long, field = "code", by = "session_id",                        similarity = "jaccard", threshold = 0.1)

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: estimation (EBICglasso, Ising, MGM) delegated ‘psychnets’ package; igraph, qgraph, bootnet needed.
code: net_gl <- build_network(srl_strategies, method = "glasso") net_gl  predictability(net_gl)   # R-squared per node from network structure

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: build_mlvar() estimates three networks simultaneously ESM/EMA diary data — three pillars mlVAR analysis single function call: Temporal (directed) — lagged fixed effects: predicts across time Contemporaneous (undirected) — partial correlations within-person residuals: moves together right now -subjects (undirected) — partial correlations person means: differs estimates match mlVAR::mlVAR() estimator = "lmer" fixed temporal contemporaneous effects. build_mlvar() needs long panel one row per beep (id, optional day, beep, variables); see ?build_mlvar runnable simulated panel.
code: # esm: one row per person-beep, columns id, day, beep, happy, calm, tired fit <- build_mlvar(esm, vars = c("happy", "calm", "tired"),                    id = "id", day = "day", beep = "beep")  fit           # the temporal, contemporaneous and between-person networks summary(fit) coefs(fit)    # tidy data.frame: beta, SE, t, p, CI for every edge

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: build_gimme() estimates separate network person using Group Iterative Mean Estimation (GIMME) algorithm, aggregates group-level picture. Use -person heterogeneity matters single group network average meaningfully different individuals.
code: # panel: one row per person-time point, columns id, V1, ..., V4 (see ?build_gimme) fit_g <- build_gimme(panel, vars = c("V1", "V2", "V3", "V4"), id = "id") fit_g   # group-level paths and the per-person networks

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: build_clusters() partitions sequences k groups using pairwise distance matrices. Supports 9 distance metrics, PAM 8 hierarchical linkage methods. build_clusters() build_mmm() results pass directly build_network(), returns one network per cluster.
code: clust <- build_clusters(net, k = 3, dissimilarity = "hamming", method = "ward.D2") plot(clust, type = "silhouette") cluster_nets <- build_network(clust, method = "tna")

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: build_mmm() discovers latent subgroups sequences share similar transition dynamics via EM — without pre-labelling groups. BIC/AIC/ICL model selection via compare_mmm().
code: mmm   <- build_mmm(net, k = 3) compare_mmm(net, k = 2:4)   # BIC / AIC / ICL per k mmm_nets <- build_network(mmm, method = "tna")

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: build_mcml() decomposes network macro (-cluster) micro (within-cluster) layers nodes belong known groups — three code families human_long.
code: families <- list(Directive     = c("Command", "Request", "Specify"),                  Evaluative    = c("Correct", "Frustrate", "Refine", "Verify"),                  Metacognitive = c("Inquire", "Interrupt")) mcml <- build_mcml(human_long, clusters = families, action = "code",                    actor = "session_id", time = "timestamp") summary(mcml)          # within and between totals per family macro_network(mcml)    # the family-level transition network

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: Capture dependencies beyond first-order transitions:
code: hon  <- build_hon(net, max_order = 2) pathways(hon)                      # arrow-notation path strings hypa <- build_hypa(net) summary(hypa)                      # over- and under-represented paths with p-values

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: Go beyond edges — find cliques, holes, high-order connectivity using tools algebraic topology.
code: sc <- build_simplicial(net, type = "clique") betti_numbers(sc)          # connected components, cycles, voids euler_characteristic(sc) ph <- persistent_homology(net)  # track topology across thresholds plot(ph) qa <- q_analysis(sc)       # Atkin's Q-connectivity structure vectors

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: Visualize raw sequence data index plots state distribution charts — clustering.
code: # Sequence heatmap: one row per sequence, coloured by state, sorted by similarity sequence_plot(net)  # After clustering: faceted by cluster clust <- build_clusters(net, k = 3) sequence_plot(clust, type = "index")  # State distribution over time distribution_plot(net, geom = "area") distribution_plot(clust, geom = "bar")

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: sequence_compare() extracts k-gram patterns grouped sequences, counts per-group frequencies, tests statistical differences via permutation — answering question “groups actually behave differently, ?”
code: res <- sequence_compare(group_nets, sub = 2:4, test = "chisq", adjust = "fdr") summary(res)                        # per-pattern frequencies + p-values plot(res)                           # back-to-back pyramid chart plot(res, style = "heatmap")        # heatmap for many patterns

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: association_rules() mines “B” patterns sequences binary matrices using Apriori algorithm. Returns support, confidence, lift, conviction every rule threshold. binary transaction matrix (rows = transactions, columns = items) accepted well.
code: rules <- association_rules(net, min_support = 0.05, min_confidence = 0.6) summary(rules)                    # tidy data.frame, sorted by lift pathways(rules)                   # rules as arrow-notation strings

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: predict_links() scores unobserved node pairs using structural similarity, identifying missing connections likely exist. evaluate_links() computes AUC, precision, recall held-edges.
code: # Keep only transitions with probability >= 0.1, then predict the rest sparse <- build_network(human_long, method = "tna", action = "code",                         actor = "session_id", time = "timestamp",                         threshold = 0.1) preds <- predict_links(sparse)    # common neighbours, Adamic-Adar, Katz, ... summary(preds)  # Do the predictions recover the weaker transitions (>= 0.05) that were cut? evaluate_links(preds, extract_edges(net, threshold = 0.05))

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: markov_stability() reports, per state, sticky (persistence, sojourn time), much long run takes (stationary probability, return time) quickly reached states. passage_time() computes mean first-passage time every pair states.
code: stab <- markov_stability(net) summary(stab)             # one row per state plot(stab)  pt <- passage_time(net) pt                        # expected steps to reach state j from state i plot(pt)

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: Every network type shares validation pipeline.
code: # Bootstrap confidence intervals boot <- bootstrap_network(net, iter = 1000) summary(boot)  # Permutation test: do high and low achievers differ? perm <- permutation(group_nets, iter = 1000) summary(perm)  # Network Comparison Test (NCT): formal test of structure + global strength nct_res <- nct(head(srl_strategies, 125), tail(srl_strategies, 125), iter = 500) nct_res                   # M (structure), S (global strength), per-edge p-values  # Split-half reliability network_reliability(net)  # Centrality stability (CS-coefficient) centrality_stability(net)  # Glasso-specific bootstrap (edge inclusion + centrality CIs) boot_gl <- boot_glasso(net_gl, iter = 1000) summary(boot_gl)

CEC flattens groups pairs clique expansion takes eigenvector centrality pairwise graph. ZEC HEC work hyperedges directly: node's score grows product scores members hyperedge belongs . reads net_hypergraph build_hypergraph() bipartite_groups(). variants can rank nodes differently, since CEC counts shared memberships pair pair ZEC HEC weigh group whole. ZEC HEC defined uniform hypergraphs , every hyperedge two members size. disconnected hypergraph, compare scores within one component: CEC gives zero every component whose leading eigenvalue largest, Z-eigenvector unique. hypergraph_measures() describes structure scores come .

title: Hypergraph eigenvector centralities — hypergraph_centrality
text:
Clique-motif eigenvector centrality (CEC) leading eigenvector clique-expanded pairwise graph \(W\) \(W_{ij} = |\{e : , j \e\}|\), number hyperedges two nodes share. reads membership , incidence weights ignored: equals igraph::eigen_centrality() clique_expansion(hg, weighted = FALSE), clique_expansion()'s default output unweighted hypergraph. vector solved directly symmetric eigendecomposition connected component (Perron-Frobenius makes leading eigenvalue connected component simple), power iteration, oscillates clique expansion bipartite (example star pairs). several components share largest eigenvalue, result projection uniform vector onto joint leading eigenspace; components smaller leading eigenvalue score zero. Z-eigenvector centrality (ZEC) solves eigen-equation hyperedge tensor, $$\lambda\, x_i \;=\; \sum_{e 
i }\; \prod_{j \e,\; j 
eq } x_j,$$ shifted power iteration (variant SS-HOPM, Kolda & Mayo, 2011, normalises tensor step adding shift). Tensor products normalisation evaluated log space, centralities stay finite normalised large hyperedges. Besides step tolerance, iteration checks eigen-equation residual small (relative residual max(sqrt(tol), 1e-6)); otherwise warns. H-eigenvector centrality (HEC) solves, iteration, $$\lambda\, x_i^{k-1} \;=\; \sum_{e 
i }\; \prod_{j \e,\; j 
eq } x_j.$$ Uniform hypergraphs . Benson (2019) defines ZEC HEC \(k\)-uniform hypergraphs. mixed sizes right-hand side mixes polynomial degrees, equation scale-free solution: vector satisfies normalisation chosen inside iteration. Hyperedges one member contribute nothing ignored uniformity check. mixed sizes use "clique", keep one size build_hypergraph() (include_pairwise = FALSE). Disconnected hypergraphs. Z-eigenvector unique hypergraph several components: different iterations can solve equation different vectors, compare "Z" values within one connected hypergraph .
